title: Model Incident Response and Recovery
summary: Detect, contain, diagnose, recover, communicate, and learn from incidents across self-hosted model artifacts, endpoints, infrastructure, data, policy, and operations.
objectives: Classify self-hosted model incidents by impact and failed system boundary rather than by surface symptom.
Contain unsafe output, unauthorized access, data exposure, cost, saturation, and bad releases while preserving useful evidence.
Use a decision-ready runbook to reconcile state, restore service, validate recovery objectives, and communicate responsibly.
Convert incident evidence into owned evaluation, control, capacity, lifecycle, and runbook improvements.

sections.title: Detect impact and declare deliberately
paragraphs: Signals can begin with failed quality checks, unsafe or unsupported output, access denials, unusual resource use, queue growth, latency, cost, artifact mismatch, telemetry loss, or user reports. Correlate the request, exact serving build, policy decision, infrastructure, and outcome before assuming that every symptom is a model failure.

Set severity from actual and credible potential impact to people, data, authorization, external actions, service, money, and legal or safety duties. Name an incident lead, evidence owner, technical responders, communications owner, and decision authority. Record confirmed facts separately from hypotheses.

Instructor narration: Start by separating observations from conclusions. In the worked scenario, release rel-2026-09-21.3 is expected to serve artifact sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa, but gpu-node-07 reports sha256:bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb. Queue delay has risen, quality case quality-03 has failed, and request req-pay-7 timed out after invoking an external payment adapter. These are confirmed fixture observations. They do not prove that the model caused the queue delay, that the identity mismatch caused the quality failure, or that the payment failed.

Worked severity declaration: Declare exercise severity SEV-1 because req-pay-7 has an unknown financial outcome and the artifact mismatch creates a credible wider integrity risk. SEV-1 is a local scenario convention, not a universal industry scale. Assign incident lead I. Chen, evidence owner R. Singh, serving responder A. Okafor, external-action responder M. Diaz, communications owner J. Park, and decision authority S. Laurent. Publish updates every 15 minutes until containment, then every 30 minutes during monitored recovery.

Initial fact record at 10:02:00Z: incident INC-42; expected release rel-2026-09-21.3; expected artifact digest sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa; observed node gpu-node-07; observed digest sha256:bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb; queue p95 delay 48,000 ms; request req-pay-7; action create-payment; target order-8842; principal svc-checkout; observed outcome unknown. The delay and threshold values in this lesson are deterministic exercise data, not production recommendations.

Ecosystem transfer: Keep model family, artifact, tokenizer, runtime, image, driver stack, adapter, policy bundle, and API contract as separate identities. Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Microsoft Phi, and NVIDIA model or serving projects must not be treated as having interchangeable artifact formats, chat templates, licenses, tool semantics, quantization support, endpoints, or security controls. Consult the first-party documentation for the exact family and runtime actually deployed. This provider-neutral lesson does not claim family-equivalent capabilities.

sections.title: Contain impact while preserving evidence
paragraphs: Contain at the narrowest effective boundary: reject a workload, disable a route or tool, revoke a principal or secret, quarantine an artifact, stop a rollout, reduce concurrency, isolate a node or site, require manual approval, or switch to a separately evaluated fallback. Do not let automatic retries amplify load or repeat uncertain side effects.

Preserve secret-safe timestamps, correlation identifiers, exact versions, digests, policy decisions, redacted logs, metrics, traces, queue state, deployment history, approvals, and observed postconditions. Follow retention and privacy policy; an incident is not permission to collect prompts, personal data, credentials, or hidden reasoning without necessity.

Instructor narration: Containment should stop the credible harm without destroying evidence or unnecessarily disabling unrelated service. For INC-42, stop release rel-2026-09-21.3, remove gpu-node-07 from routing, quarantine its artifact, place only create-payment in reconciliation-only mode, and pause automatic retries for unknown outcomes. Preserve read-only queue and deployment snapshots before changing them. Route unaffected traffic to a fallback only if that exact fallback and contract were evaluated previously.

Privacy-conscious evidence ledger: retain correlation IDs, timestamps, release and image identifiers, artifact and configuration digests, policy decisions, redacted error categories, queue depth and age, deployment events, adapter request IDs, and authoritative external status. Do not copy raw prompts, credentials, payment details, personal data, or hidden reasoning into the exercise record. Apply organizational access and retention rules and record evidence access. The retention duration is UNKNOWN because no organizational policy was supplied.

Containment record at 10:05:00Z: rollout paused; gpu-node-07 removed from service; create-payment placed in reconciliation-only mode; automatic retries disabled for unknown outcomes; admission reduced for the affected workload; artifact directories made read-only; snapshots assigned to evidence owner R. Singh. No rollback, retry, or compensation is authorized by this record.

Container and cluster settings are evidence to inspect, not proof of deployed safety. Docker documents that containers have no resource constraints by default, so explicit limits and host capacity matter. The Kubernetes security checklist provides configuration guidance but does not establish that a particular cluster enforces it. Sources: https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/resource_constraints/ and https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/security-checklist/, verified 2026-09-21.

sections.title: Diagnose the first failed boundary
paragraphs: Test artifact integrity and provenance, runtime and driver compatibility, endpoint and adapter contracts, identity and authorization, network and secret access, evaluation behavior, data and prompt inputs, capacity and scheduling, dependencies, telemetry, and recent change history. More than one boundary may fail, and a fluent response can conceal a serious control failure.

For unknown outcomes, reconcile the system of record before retrying or compensating. Use evidence to distinguish transient, deterministic, policy, authorization, corrupt-state, capacity, and incompatible-release failures because each allows different recovery actions.

Instructor narration: Test one boundary at a time and record the expected identity, observation, evidence source, conclusion, and next action. A queue increase following a release does not identify the model, scheduler, adapter, or dependency as the cause. The matrix prevents a plausible story from becoming an unsupported root-cause statement.

Boundary diagnostic matrix for INC-42: Artifact integrity expects rel-2026-09-21.3 and digest sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa; gpu-node-07 reports sha256:bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb, so quarantine it and verify provenance. Runtime compatibility expects image registry.example.invalid/serving@sha256:cccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccc and fixture contract fixture-v1; the snapshot matches, so runtime incompatibility is not established. Authorization expects svc-checkout to have only create-payment access; the snapshot shows that grant, but access does not prove action completion. Evaluation expects quality-01 through quality-04 to pass; quality-03 fails on the bad release. Capacity expects queue age below the exercise recovery threshold of 5,000 ms; observed age is 48,000 ms. Telemetry expects correlated serving, queue, policy, and adapter events; the adapter result is missing. Cost expects the exercise budget guard to remain true; it does, but that cannot override another failed boundary.

Reconciliation matrix: Compare incident ID, request ID, action, target, identity, authority, observation time, and final outcome. Missing, stale, future-dated, non-authoritative, wrong-request, wrong-action, wrong-target, or wrong-identity evidence means hold. Partial or pending evidence means hold. Matching authoritative fresh success means mark completed and never repeat. Matching authoritative fresh failure can make a new attempt eligible only if all recovery gates and RTO/RPO objectives also pass. Eligibility does not execute or approve the action.

Worked reasoning: req-pay-7 has action create-payment, target order-8842, identity svc-checkout, and no authoritative final evidence. A timeout is not evidence of failure. Retrying could duplicate a payment, while compensating could reverse an action that never occurred. The justified decision is HOLD_RECONCILE. This is not deny-all: matching authoritative success becomes COMPLETED, and a distinct valid request with authoritative failure can become RETRY_ALLOWED after every recovery gate and objective passes.

Provider transfer: Repeat this matrix using the exact identities and contracts for the deployed Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Microsoft Phi, NVIDIA, or other model and runtime combination. Do not transfer a result merely because two systems generate text. MLPerf Inference compares defined workloads and measured systems; this fictional lab has no benchmark score and makes no performance-equivalence claim. Source: https://mlcommons.org/benchmarks/inference-datacenter/, verified 2026-09-21.

sections.title: Recover to explicit objectives
paragraphs: Choose a tested action: remove traffic, restart a bounded component, replace a corrupt artifact, rotate a secret, restore configuration or state, scale within a safe envelope, fail over, roll back the complete serving unit, or keep service unavailable pending human decision. Define recovery-time and recovery-point objectives where durable state is involved.

Validate exact model and dependency identity, authorization, representative quality and safety cases, endpoint compatibility, capacity, queues, telemetry, alerts, cost, and user-visible postconditions. Restore traffic in bounded stages and watch for recurrence; a green health endpoint alone does not prove recovery.

Instructor narration: Recovery is a gated decision, not a restart. For INC-42, keep the external-action route held, replace the quarantined serving unit with the previously evaluated complete unit, verify every identity, handle queued work according to policy, and restore traffic in bounded stages. Do not act on req-pay-7 until its authoritative outcome is reconciled.

Recovery objectives for the deterministic exercise are RTO 600,000 ms and RPO 300,000 ms. RTO actual is recoveredAtMs minus declaredAtMs: 1,720,000,420,000 minus 1,720,000,000,000 equals 420,000 ms, which passes. RPO actual is incidentAtMs minus checkpointAtMs: 1,720,000,000,000 minus 1,719,999,880,000 equals 120,000 ms, which passes. These values are fixtures. A real organization must define restoration and recoverable durable state for its service.

Complete recovery gate: Identity verifies model, tokenizer, configuration, runtime, image, adapter, and policy digests. Access verifies intended principals and removal of temporary privilege. Quality verifies representative quality, safety, and action-policy cases. Compatibility verifies endpoint, schema, tokenizer, adapter, driver, and client contracts. Capacity verifies limits, scheduling, queues, and bounded-load behavior. Telemetry verifies correlated logs, metrics, traces, alerts, and external-action status. Cost verifies budget and retry-amplification controls. User service verifies completion, error behavior, and downstream postconditions. Every gate and both objectives must pass before a new action can be labeled RETRY_ALLOWED. Deny-all is not recovery because it fails user service.

Worked recovery evidence at 10:09:00Z: the known-good unit reports expected artifact, tokenizer, configuration, runtime, image, adapter, and policy identities; svc-checkout has only its intended grant; quality-01 through quality-04 pass; endpoint fixture-v1 passes; queue age is 3,100 ms; correlated telemetry is present; budget guard is true; and non-action user checks pass. The payment route remains held because req-pay-7 is unreconciled. Recovery is therefore explicitly scoped rather than falsely declared complete.

Runnable repair lab from the repository root:

The lab requires Node.js 22, native ESM, no dependencies, no API keys, and no network. Before repair, the first decision is RETRY_ALLOWED with exit 0 and the test summary is `RESULT 17 passed, 6 failed` with exit 1. After repair, the first decision is HOLD_RECONCILE with exit 2, tests print `RESULT 23 passed, 0 failed` with exit 0, and the changed input remains RETRY_ALLOWED with exit 0. Exact JSON and complete test stdout are in the README.

Prediction before answer: Predict the decisions for missing, stale, future-dated, wrong-identity, non-authoritative, partial, duplicate-completed, failed-gate, RTO-miss, RPO-miss, and changed-retryable inputs. Identify which fact establishes completion, failure, or continued uncertainty. Record the prediction before reading the answer key or reference.

Learner task: Edit only `training/self-hosted-model-operations/model-incident-response-and-recovery/lab/src/starter.mjs`. Repair the two assignments in the single deliberately defective unknown-outcome branch. Preserve strict validation, immutable completed-history handling, recovery gates, objectives, output schema, and exit codes. Do not edit tests, fixtures, validation, or reference files. Do not import the reference or replace the decision with a blanket hold.

Explained answer key: Missing evidence leaves success and failure possible. Stale or future-dated evidence is not timely evidence for the decision. Wrong-identity evidence concerns another actor. Non-authoritative evidence cannot settle the system of record. Partial evidence is not final. All therefore hold. Completed history and matching authoritative success return COMPLETED and never repeat, even though that historical status is not permission for a new action. Matching authoritative failure permits RETRY_ALLOWED only when every gate and both objectives pass. A failed access gate, any other failed gate, an RTO miss, or an RPO miss blocks new action eligibility and exits 3. The changed req-pay-8 fixture remains retryable, proving that deny-all is invalid.

sections.title: Communicate, close, and improve
paragraphs: Updates state time, scope, impact, confirmed facts, current containment, service status, next decision, and expected update cadence. Follow organizational privacy, legal, customer, and regulatory obligations. Avoid unsupported root-cause claims and never expose sensitive operational evidence.

Close only after impact has stopped, recovery evidence passes, stakeholders receive required communication, temporary access is removed, and follow-up work has owners and dates. Build a blameless timeline, identify contributing conditions, add reproducing cases, improve controls, rehearse the revised runbook, and measure recurrence.

Instructor narration: A useful update tells stakeholders what is known, what remains uncertain, and which decision comes next. It does not publish raw evidence or declare root cause merely because rollback improved symptoms. Continue the announced cadence until the incident lead changes it explicitly.

Stakeholder update at 10:10:00Z: `INC-42 remains SEV-1. Scope includes release rel-2026-09-21.3 on gpu-node-07, elevated queue delay, and create-payment request req-pay-7 with an unknown external outcome. We paused the rollout, quarantined the mismatched artifact, removed the node from routing, and disabled retries for unknown external actions. A known-good serving unit passes identity, access, quality, compatibility, capacity, telemetry, cost, and non-action user-service checks. The payment route remains in reconciliation-only mode. No root cause is confirmed. The next decision depends on authoritative payment-system evidence for req-pay-7. Next update: 10:25:00Z.`

Exercise timeline: 10:00:00Z release rel-2026-09-21.3 begins. 10:01:30Z queue alarm fires. 10:02:00Z digest mismatch and req-pay-7 timeout are correlated. 10:03:00Z INC-42 is declared SEV-1 and roles assigned. 10:05:00Z rollout, node, route, retry, and evidence containment complete. 10:07:00Z quality-03 failure reproduced in the fixture. 10:09:00Z known-good unit passes gates for non-action traffic. 10:10:00Z stakeholder update issued. 10:12:00Z the authoritative system of record reports req-pay-7 succeeded with matching request, action, target, and identity, so it is marked completed and never retried. 10:15:00Z a distinct synthetic canary passes. 10:20:00Z bounded restoration completes. 10:35:00Z no recurrence is observed during the exercise window.

Closure decision: Close at 10:40:00Z only after impact has stopped, req-pay-7 is reconciled as completed, all eight recovery gates and both objectives pass for restored scope, required communication is sent, temporary access is removed, and prevention work has owners and dates. This is simulated closure. It is not evidence of a real incident, execution, approval, payment, deployment, or production recovery.

Owned prevention backlog: A. Okafor owns admission-time verification of artifact, tokenizer, configuration, runtime, image, adapter, and policy identities by 2026-10-05. R. Singh owns the redacted reconciliation schema and access review by 2026-10-08. M. Diaz owns idempotency and authoritative-status contract tests by 2026-10-12. J. Park owns the stakeholder update template by 2026-10-01. I. Chen owns queue saturation rehearsal and bounded rollback drill by 2026-10-15. S. Laurent owns closure-evidence and temporary-access review by 2026-10-16. Names and dates are exercise data.

Rubric: A complete submission states impact-based severity, roles, and cadence; applies narrow containment; records privacy-conscious evidence; diagnoses artifact, runtime, identity, evaluation, capacity, dependency, and telemetry boundaries; reconciles every uncertain action before retry, rollback, or compensation; verifies all eight gates and both objectives; calculates RTO and RPO; supplies a timeline, stakeholder update, closure decision, and owned prevention work; repairs only the deliberate branch; passes immutable literal-oracle tests; and still permits the changed valid input. Blanket HOLD, blanket RETRY, altered fixtures, edited tests, deleted validation, or importing the private reference does not pass.

activity.title: Run a self-hosted model incident exercise
instructions: Use a scenario combining a bad model release, elevated queue delay, an artifact identity mismatch, and an uncertain user-visible outcome.
Declare severity, roles, communication cadence, containment actions, and evidence-preservation boundaries.
Build a boundary-by-boundary diagnostic table and reconcile every unknown outcome before retry, rollback, or compensation.
Execute the recovery runbook against stated recovery objectives and verify identity, access, quality, compatibility, capacity, telemetry, cost, and user-visible service.
Produce the incident timeline, stakeholder update, closure decision, and owned prevention backlog.

Before reading the answer key, predict results for missing, stale, future, wrong-identity, non-authoritative, partial, duplicate-completed, each failed recovery gate, RTO miss, RPO miss, and the changed valid input.
From the repository root, run the starter, immutable tests, and changed-input command. Edit only `training/self-hosted-model-operations/model-incident-response-and-recovery/lab/src/starter.mjs`.

Submit the repaired file and a causal explanation that a timeout creates uncertainty, uncertainty is not failure, repeated side effects can cause duplicate harm, completed history is not new-action permission, and matching final evidence plus successful recovery gates and objectives is required for a retry.
evidence: A severity decision, role assignment, containment record, and privacy-conscious evidence ledger.
A diagnostic and reconciliation matrix tied to exact build and infrastructure identities.
A recovery-objective validation report, communication record, timeline, and owned improvement plan.
Recorded predictions, repaired starter output, `RESULT 23 passed, 0 failed` with exit 0, changed-input RETRY_ALLOWED output with exit 0, and an explanation of why deny-all is invalid.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which apparently harmless symptom could indicate the largest hidden blast radius in your environment?

choices: Actual and credible potential impact to people, data, authorization, service, money, and obligations
questions.explanation: Severity follows impact, not presentation or system size.

questions.prompt: What is the best first containment?
choices: The narrowest effective control that stops ongoing impact
questions.explanation: Targeted containment limits harm while preserving unaffected service and evidence.

questions.prompt: A timeout leaves a user-visible action uncertain. What comes next?
choices: Reconcile the system of record and observed postcondition
questions.explanation: Unknown outcomes must be reconciled before another side effect.

questions.prompt: Which evidence policy is appropriate during an incident?
choices: Collect every prompt and secret forever
questions.explanation: Incident response still requires data minimization, privacy, and secret protection.

questions.prompt: Why is a healthy endpoint insufficient recovery evidence?
choices: It may not prove identity, access, quality, queues, downstream effects, telemetry, or user-visible service
questions.explanation: Recovery must validate the complete service contract and effects.

choices: When the model says it is fixed
After containment, validated recovery, required communication, access cleanup, and owned follow-up
questions.explanation: Closure requires evidence and accountable prevention work.

cues.text:
Welcome. An unsafe answer, timeout, queue
alarm, access denial, cost spike, or

artifact mismatch is a signal, not a root
cause. In this class, you will

declare severity from impact, contain the
narrowest effective boundary, diagnose the

first failure, reconcile uncertain
effects, recover to explicit objectives,

communicate confirmed facts, and turn the
incident into owned prevention work.

Detect impact and declare deliberately.
Signals can begin with failed quality or

safety checks, unsupported output,
authorization denials, unusual resource

use, queue growth, latency, cost, artifact
identity mismatch, telemetry loss, a bad

deployment, or a user report. Correlate
the request, exact serving build, policy

decision, infrastructure, dependency
state, and observed outcome before calling

every symptom a model failure. Set
severity from actual and credible

potential impact to people, data,
authorization, external actions, service,

money, and legal or safety duties. A
fluent answer can conceal unauthorized

access, while a visible timeout may have
no lasting effect or may hide a

completed external action. Name an
incident lead, evidence owner, technical

responders, communications owner, and
decision authority. Establish an update

cadence and one decision log. Record
confirmed facts, observations, and

timestamps separately from hypotheses.
NIST's incident-response recommendations

integrate preparation and response with
broader cybersecurity risk management; use

that discipline to make roles, evidence,
decisions, and recovery expectations ready
before an emergency.

Consider a synthetic incident after a
model rollout. Queue delay rises, one

replica reports the candidate alias but an
old artifact digest, and a user says

an action timed out. Confirmed facts are
limited: queue delay exceeded the

objective, identity is inconsistent, and
the client did not receive completion. It

is not yet confirmed whether the external
action occurred or whether the weights

caused the delay. Severity accounts for
the credible duplicate-action and

authorization impact, not merely the
visible latency. The incident lead assigns

an evidence owner, serving responder,
application responder, communications

owner, and rollback authority. The first
update states the time, affected route,

current uncertainty, bounded containment,
service status, and next decision. This

prevents a fluent but unsupported
root-cause story from replacing the
investigation.

Contain at the narrowest boundary that
reliably stops ongoing impact. Reject one

workload, disable a route or tool, revoke
a principal or secret, quarantine an

artifact, stop a rollout, reduce
concurrency, isolate a node or site,

require manual approval, or switch to a
separately evaluated fallback. Keep

service unavailable when no safe mode
exists. Prevent automatic retries from

multiplying load or repeating uncertain
side effects. Preserve evidence without

creating another incident. Capture
necessary timestamps, bounded correlation

identifiers, exact release and artifact
identities, digests, policy decisions,

redacted logs, metrics, traces, queue
state, deployment history, approvals,

configuration changes, and observed
postconditions. Follow retention, privacy,

legal-hold, and access policy. An incident
is not permission to collect every prompt,

response, personal identifier, credential,
secret, or hidden reasoning. OpenTelemetry

conventions can help correlate signals,
but your application-owned contract and

evidence policy determine which fields are
justified and safe.

Diagnose the first failed boundary with
evidence. Test artifact integrity and

provenance; runtime, driver, and library
compatibility; endpoint and adapter

contracts; identity and object or function
authorization; network and secret access;

evaluation behavior; prompt, retrieval,
and data inputs; capacity, placement, and

queues; dependencies; telemetry; and
recent change history. More than one

boundary can fail. A bad release may
create memory pressure, which creates

queueing, which triggers unsafe retries,
while an identity mismatch makes

attribution harder. Classify evidence as
transient, deterministic, policy,

authorization, corrupt-state, capacity,
dependency, telemetry, or

incompatible-release failure because each
permits different recovery. For any

unknown external or user-visible outcome,
query the authoritative system of record

and observed postcondition before
retrying, compensating, or declaring

success. A client timeout proves that the
client did not receive completion; it does

not prove that downstream work did not
happen.

Checkpoint. A tool call times out after
the request left the model service. The

user sees an error, but the external
system may have completed the action.

Should the service retry, and what
evidence must come first?
Hold the checkpoint for up to seventy-five seconds with pause, extend, and continue controls.

Do not retry merely because the caller saw
a timeout. Correlate the exact request

and operation, query the external system
of record, inspect the durable

postcondition, and determine whether the
action completed, failed, or remains

uncertain. Only then choose no action, an
idempotent or otherwise safe retry, or an

authorized compensating operation.
Preserve the reconciliation and decision

without exposing unnecessary content. If
your answer retried immediately, it could

duplicate a financial, administrative,
communication, or data-changing action.

The safe sequence is reconcile, authorize,
act, and verify.

Recover to explicit objectives. Choose a
tested action: remove traffic, restart one

bounded component, replace a corrupt
artifact, rotate and revoke a secret,

restore configuration or durable state,
scale within an evaluated envelope, fail

over, roll back the complete serving unit,
or remain unavailable pending human

authority. Where durable state exists,
state recovery-time and recovery-point

objectives and the evidence that proves
them. Validate the complete service

contract: exact model and dependency
identity, authentication and

authorization, representative quality and
safety cases, endpoint compatibility,

capacity and queue state, telemetry and
alerting, cost behavior, reconciled

external effects, and user-visible
postconditions. Restore traffic in bounded

stages with an observation window and
recurrence stop condition. A green

liveness endpoint proves only that one
process can answer its health check. It

does not prove the correct model, safe
access, valid outcomes, cleared queues,

consistent state, working telemetry, or
restored user service.

Communicate what is confirmed. Each update
states time, known scope and impact,

current containment, service status, next
decision, and expected update cadence.

Follow organizational privacy, legal,
customer, contractual, and regulatory

duties. Avoid unsupported root-cause
claims and never publish sensitive

operational evidence. Close only after
impact has stopped, recovery

postconditions pass, required stakeholders
are informed, temporary access and

emergency controls are removed, and
follow-up work has owners and dates. Build

a blameless timeline that identifies
contributing conditions rather than

searching for one person to blame. Add
privacy-reviewed reproducing cases,

strengthen identity, capacity, telemetry,
release, backup, or rollback controls,

update the runbook, rehearse the revised
response, and measure recurrence. A

resolved alert without validated recovery
and owned prevention is not incident
closure.

Now run the incident exercise. Use the
scenario combining a bad release, queue

delay, artifact identity mismatch, and
uncertain user-visible effect. Declare

severity, roles, cadence, containment, and
evidence boundaries. Build the boundary

diagnostic table and reconcile every
unknown outcome before retry, rollback, or

compensation. Execute the recovery runbook
against explicit objectives. Verify exact

identity, access, quality, compatibility,
capacity, queues, telemetry, cost, and

user-visible service. Produce the
timeline, stakeholder update, closure

decision, reproducing cases, and
prevention backlog with owners and dates.
Provide one hundred eighty seconds of optional work time with pause, extend, save, and continue controls.

Begin the check when you can set severity
from impact, select narrow containment,

reconcile a timeout, preserve governed
evidence, validate more than endpoint

health, and define evidence-based closure.
The check starts only when you choose
Begin knowledge check.

Remember: respond to impact, contain
narrowly, preserve only justified

evidence, diagnose the boundary, reconcile
unknown effects, and call service

recovered only when the complete contract
passes.

Execute the recovery runbook against explicit objectives. Verify exact identity, access, quality, compatibility, capacity, queues, telemetry, cost, and user-visible service. Produce the timeline, stakeholder update, closure decision, reproducing cases, and prevention backlog with owners and dates.

reliably stops ongoing impact. Reject one

workload, disable a route or tool, revoke
a principal or secret, quarantine an

artifact, stop a rollout, reduce
concurrency, isolate a node or site,

require manual approval, or switch to a
separately evaluated fallback. Keep

service unavailable when no safe mode
exists. Prevent automatic retries from

multiplying load or repeating uncertain
side effects. Preserve evidence without

creating another incident. Capture
necessary timestamps, bounded correlation

identifiers, exact release and artifact
identities, digests, policy decisions,

redacted logs, metrics, traces, queue
state, deployment history, approvals,

configuration changes, and observed
postconditions. Follow retention, privacy,

legal-hold, and access policy. An incident
is not permission to collect every prompt,

response, personal identifier, credential,
secret, or hidden reasoning. OpenTelemetry

conventions can help correlate signals,
but your application-owned contract and

evidence policy determine which fields are
justified and safe.

Diagnose the first failed boundary with
evidence. Test artifact integrity and

provenance; runtime, driver, and library
compatibility; endpoint and adapter

contracts; identity and object or function
authorization; network and secret access;

evaluation behavior; prompt, retrieval,
and data inputs; capacity, placement, and

queues; dependencies; telemetry; and
recent change history. More than one

boundary can fail. A bad release may
create memory pressure, which creates

queueing, which triggers unsafe retries,
while an identity mismatch makes

attribution harder. Classify evidence as
transient, deterministic, policy,

authorization, corrupt-state, capacity,
dependency, telemetry, or

incompatible-release failure because each
permits different recovery. For any

unknown external or user-visible outcome,
query the authoritative system of record

and observed postcondition before
retrying, compensating, or declaring

success. A client timeout proves that the
client did not receive completion; it does

not prove that downstream work did not
happen.

Checkpoint. A tool call times out after
the request left the model service. The

user sees an error, but the external
system may have completed the action.

Should the service retry, and what
evidence must come first?

Do not retry merely because the caller saw
a timeout. Correlate the exact request

and operation, query the external system
of record, inspect the durable

postcondition, and determine whether the
action completed, failed, or remains

uncertain. Only then choose no action, an
idempotent or otherwise safe retry, or an

authorized compensating operation.
Preserve the reconciliation and decision

without exposing unnecessary content. If
your answer retried immediately, it could

duplicate a financial, administrative,
communication, or data-changing action.

The safe sequence is reconcile, authorize,
act, and verify.

Recover to explicit objectives. Choose a
tested action: remove traffic, restart one

bounded component, replace a corrupt
artifact, rotate and revoke a secret,

restore configuration or durable state,
scale within an evaluated envelope, fail

over, roll back the complete serving unit,
or remain unavailable pending human

authority. Where durable state exists,
state recovery-time and recovery-point

objectives and the evidence that proves
them. Validate the complete service

contract: exact model and dependency
identity, authentication and

authorization, representative quality and
safety cases, endpoint compatibility,

capacity and queue state, telemetry and
alerting, cost behavior, reconciled

external effects, and user-visible
postconditions. Restore traffic in bounded

stages with an observation window and
recurrence stop condition. A green

liveness endpoint proves only that one
process can answer its health check. It

does not prove the correct model, safe
access, valid outcomes, cleared queues,

consistent state, working telemetry, or
restored user service.

Communicate what is confirmed. Each update
states time, known scope and impact,

current containment, service status, next
decision, and expected update cadence.

Follow organizational privacy, legal,
customer, contractual, and regulatory

duties. Avoid unsupported root-cause
claims and never publish sensitive

operational evidence. Close only after
impact has stopped, recovery

postconditions pass, required stakeholders
are informed, temporary access and

emergency controls are removed, and
follow-up work has owners and dates. Build

a blameless timeline that identifies
contributing conditions rather than

searching for one person to blame. Add
privacy-reviewed reproducing cases,

strengthen identity, capacity, telemetry,
release, backup, or rollback controls,

update the runbook, rehearse the revised
response, and measure recurrence. A

resolved alert without validated recovery
and owned prevention is not incident
closure.

Now run the incident exercise. Use the
scenario combining a bad release, queue

delay, artifact identity mismatch, and
uncertain user-visible effect. Declare

severity, roles, cadence, containment, and
evidence boundaries. Build the boundary

diagnostic table and reconcile every
unknown outcome before retry, rollback, or

compensation. Execute the recovery runbook
against explicit objectives. Verify exact

identity, access, quality, compatibility,
capacity, queues, telemetry, cost, and

user-visible service. Produce the
timeline, stakeholder update, closure

decision, reproducing cases, and
prevention backlog with owners and dates.

Begin the check when you can set severity
from impact, select narrow containment,

reconcile a timeout, preserve governed
evidence, validate more than endpoint

health, and define evidence-based closure.
The check starts only when you choose
Begin knowledge check.

Remember: respond to impact, contain
narrowly, preserve only justified

evidence, diagnose the boundary, reconcile
unknown effects, and call service

recovered only when the complete contract
passes.

effects, recover to explicit objectives, communicate confirmed facts, and turn the
incident into owned prevention work. Detect impact and declare deliberately.
